claims.source: The offset of optogenetic inactivation was followed by rebound excitation in a light dose-dependent manner, limiting temporal resolution.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing removal of photoinhibition elevated spike rate above baseline, with rebound activity depending on both photostimulus duration and intensity (Figure 12A-C).

claims.claim: Blue light is highly confined in cortical tissue with light intensity dropping to less than 20% at 500 µm below the surface of the brain.
claims.source: Light intensity attenuated rapidly as a function of depth, to less than 20% at 500 µm below the surface of the brain (Figure 3D; depth at half max, 300 µm).
claims.evidence: Supported by photobleaching measurements in transgenic mice expressing GFP in nuclei of cortical pyramidal neurons (Figure 3A-D).

claims.claim: Blue light intensity dropped off laterally to 50% at 135 µm from the laser center.
claims.source: Laterally, light intensity dropped off to 50% at 135 µm (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Supported by photobleaching measurements showing spatial profile of blue light (Figure 3D).

claims.claim: Orange light propagated much further than blue light, with depth at half max of 846 µm.
claims.source: In contrast to blue light, orange light propagated much further (depth at half max, 846 µm), penetrating all layers of cortex and illuminating a cubic millimeter of volume (Figure 3E–G), 28 times larger than for blue light.
claims.evidence: Supported by photobleaching measurements in transgenic mice expressing mCherry in nuclei of cortical pyramidal neurons (Figure 3E-G).

claims.claim: ChR-assisted photoinhibition in transgenic mice produced strong inactivation with >80% reduction in spike rate for putative pyramidal neurons with low laser powers (0.5–1.5 mW).
claims.source: Near the center of the photostimulus (<0.4 mm from laser center), ChR-assisted photoinhibition in transgenic mice produced strong inactivation, with >80% of reduction in spike rate for putative pyramidal neurons with low laser powers (0.5–1.5 mW, Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by silicon probe recordings measuring spike rates during photostimulation in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP, PV-IRES-Cre x Ai32, and other transgenic mice (Figure 1E).

claims.claim: Arch and Jaws-mediated photoinhibition required roughly 10-fold higher laser power to achieve similar silencing compared to ChR-assisted photoinhibition.
claims.source: Arch and Jaws-mediated photoinhibition required roughly 10-fold higher laser power to achieve similar silencing compared to ChR-assisted photoinhibition (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing laser power requirements across different optogenetic methods (Figure 1E).

claims.claim: For Arch-mediated photoinhibition, temporally-modulated photostimuli were more effective in silencing activity than constant photostimuli at the same average power.
claims.source: For Arch-mediated photoinhibition, temporally-modulated photostimuli were more effective in silencing activity than constant photostimuli at the same average power (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing 40 Hz sinusoid photostimulus with constant photostimulus (Figure 1F).

claims.claim: GtACR1 produced the most potent photoinhibition near the laser center, with >80% of spikes silenced at 0.1 mW.
claims.source: Under blue light (473 nm) illumination, GtACR1 produced the most potent photoinhibition near the laser center, with >80% of the spikes silenced at 0.1 mW (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Supported by silicon probe recordings in Emx1-IRES-Cre x GtACR1 mice (Figure 2C).

claims.claim: Below 0.2 mW, photostimulation of soma localized GtACR1 induced little excitation.
claims.source: Below 0.2 mW, photostimulation of soma localized GtACR1 induced little excitation (Mahn et al., 2018; Messier et al., 2018) (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate during first 20 ms of photostimulation onset (Figure 2D) and by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: At higher laser powers, transient short-latency excitation was apparent with GtACR1, which was likely due to axonal excitation.
claims.source: At higher laser powers, transient short-latency excitation was apparent, which was likely due to axonal excitation.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing axonal excitation at 0.8 mW laser power (Figure 2D) and inference based on known properties of GtACR1 expression in axons.

claims.claim: Photostimulation of ChR2 in GABAergic neurons produced nearly uniform inhibition of pyramidal neurons across cortical layers.
claims.source: Photostimulation of ChR2 in GABAergic neurons produced nearly uniform inhibition of pyramidal neurons across cortical layers (Figure 4A, VGAT-ChR2-EYFP, Sst-IRES-Cre X Ai32, and PV-IRES-Cre X Ai32), despite limited penetration of blue light in tissue (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by silicon probe recordings showing relative spike rate across cortical depth (Figure 4A) and comparison with light penetration data (Figure 3).

claims.claim: Photoinhibition removed the majority of spikes (>80%) in a column across a wide range of laser powers (1.5–14 mW).
claims.source: Photoinhibition removed the majority of spikes (>80%) in a column across a wide range of laser powers (1.5–14 mW), indicating that photoinhibition is an effective method for local inactivation.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate across cortical layers at different laser powers (Figure 4A-B).

claims.claim: At low laser powers (0.5 mW) in Sst-IRES-Cre X Ai32 mice, selective excitation of Sst neurons produced a disinhibition of excitatory neurons around layer 4.
claims.source: A notable exception was seen at low laser powers (0.5 mW) in Sst-IRES-Cre X Ai32 mice. Selective excitation of Sst neurons produced a disinhibition of excitatory neurons around layer 4 (Figure 4A, , Sst-IRES-Cre X Ai32).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased relative spike rate in layer 4 at 0.5 mW (Figure 4A) and inference based on known circuit connectivity.

claims.claim: This disinhibition in layer four was likely mediated by Sst neurons that inhibit PV neurons.
claims.source: This disinhibition in layer four was likely mediated by Sst neurons that inhibit PV neurons. Activation of Sst neurons therefore removed a major source of inhibition onto excitatory neurons (Xu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Inference based on known circuit connectivity supported by citation to Xu et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Despite different propagation of blue and orange light in tissue, ChR-assisted photoinhibition was remarkably similar for both illumination wavelengths.
claims.source: Despite different propagation of blue and orange light in tissue (Figure 3), ChR-assisted photoinhibition was remarkably similar for both illumination wavelengths.
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of photoinhibition profiles for blue light (Figure 4A) and orange light (Figure 4B) and light propagation data (Figure 3).

claims.claim: At moderate laser power (1.5 mW), blue light excited FS neurons mainly in superficial layers.
claims.source: At moderate laser power (1.5 mW), blue light excited FS neurons mainly in superficial layers (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate of FS neurons across cortical depth (Figure 4C).

claims.claim: Loss of activity was present in both superficial and deep layers despite FS neurons being excited mainly in superficial layers.
claims.source: Yet, loss of activity was present in both superficial and deep layers (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing photoinhibition across all cortical layers (Figure 4A) despite limited FS neuron excitation in deep layers (Figure 4C).

claims.claim: The profile of silencing mediated by GtACR1 was similar for blue and red light, despite profound wavelength-dependent differences of light propagation in tissue.
claims.source: Remarkably, the profile of silencing mediated by GtACR1 was also similar for blue and red light (Figure 4D–E), despite profound wavelength-dependent differences of light propagation in tissue (and much higher power levels required at the longer excitation wavelength).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of photoinhibition profiles for blue light (Figure 4D) and red light (Figure 4E) and light propagation data (Figure 3).

claims.claim: In VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, FS neurons near the laser center were activated in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.source: In VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, FS neurons near the laser center were activated in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate of FS neurons as a function of laser power (Figure 5B).

claims.claim: The lateral spread of FS neuron excitation was dependent on laser power (at 0.5 mW, half-max width, 0.15 mm; at 14 mW, 1.5 mm).
claims.source: The lateral spread of FS neuron excitation was dependent on laser power (at 0.5 mW, half-max width, 0.15 mm; at 14 mW, 1.5 mm, Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate versus lateral distance for FS neurons at different laser powers (Figure 5B).

claims.claim: A long tail in the light intensity profile can activate light gated channel more than 1 mm from the center of the laser, even for blue excitation light.
claims.source: These measurements show that a long tail in the light intensity profile can activate light gated channel more than 1 mm from the center of the laser, even for blue excitation light.
claims.evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing FS neuron excitation extending to 1.5 mm at high laser powers (Figure 5B).

claims.claim: Photoinhibition of pyramidal neurons extended 1 mm beyond the activation profile of FS neurons.
claims.source: Photoinhibition of pyramidal neurons extended 1 mm beyond the activation profile of FS neurons (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing pyramidal neuron activity was reduced even 1 mm away from the laser center where FS neurons were not activated (Figure 5B).

claims.claim: This spread of photoinhibition extends beyond typical sizes of dendritic and axonal arbors of GABAergic neurons and dendritic arbors of pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: This spread of photoinhibition extends beyond typical sizes of dendritic and axonal arbors of GABAergic neurons (Jiang et al., 2015) and dendritic arbors of pyramidal neurons (Oberlaender et al., 2012; Oswald et al., 2013; Shepherd et al., 2005; Yamashita et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Inference based on comparison of measured photoinhibition spread with known anatomical dimensions from cited literature.

claims.claim: Selectively photostimulating PV neurons produced similarly broad photoinhibition profile as photostimulating all GABAergic neurons.
claims.source: However, a similarly broad photoinhibition profile was induced in PV-IRES-Cre X Ai32 mice (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing photoinhibition profiles in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice (Figure 5B) and PV-IRES-Cre X Ai32 mice (Figure 5C).

claims.claim: Using orange light to illuminate a larger cortical volume in transgenic mice expressing ReaChR in PV neurons produced similar photoinhibition profile to photostimulating ChR2 in PV neurons using blue light.
claims.source: We next sought to produce a broader photoinhibition by using orange light to illuminate a larger cortical volume in transgenic mice expressing ReaChR in PV neurons. However, the resulting photoinhibition profile was similar to those produced by photostimulating ChR2 in PV neurons using blue light (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing photoinhibition profiles for ChR2 with blue light (Figure 5C) and ReaChR with orange light (Figure 5D).

claims.claim: Photoinhibition by selective excitation of Sst neurons induced similarly broad photoinhibition.
claims.source: First, photoinhibition by selective excitation of Sst neurons induced similarly broad photoinhibition (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing photoinhibition profile in Sst-IRES-Cre x Ai32 mice (Figure 5E).

claims.claim: Direct photoinhibition of pyramidal neurons using light-gated ion pumps induced similarly broad photoinhibition.
claims.source: Next, direct photoinhibition of pyramidal neurons using light-gated ion pumps (Emx1-IRES-Cre X Ai35D mice or Emx1-IRES-Cre X Camk2a-tTA X Ai79 mice) induced similarly broad photoinhibition (Figure 5F and G).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing photoinhibition profiles for Arch (Figure 5F) and Jaws (Figure 5G).

claims.claim: ChR-assisted photoinhibition in anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM) produced similarly broad spatial spread regardless of the method used to drive photoinhibition.
claims.source: ChR-assisted photoinhibition in a different brain region (anterior lateral motor cortex, ALM) also produced similarly broad spatial spread regardless of the method used to drive photoinhibition (Figure 5H–I, blue light photostimulation in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, or orange light photostimulation in PV-IRES-Cre X ReaChR mice).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing photoinhibition profiles in ALM for VGAT-ChR2-EYFP (Figure 5H) and PV-IRES-Cre X ReaChR (Figure 5I).

claims.claim: Across all methods, the fractional reduction in spike rate near the laser center approximately predicted the lateral spread of photoinhibition.
claims.source: Across all methods, the fractional reduction in spike rate near the laser center approximately predicted the lateral spread of photoinhibition (Figure 5J).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relationship between photoinhibition strength and spatial spread across multiple methods (Figure 5J).

claims.claim: The spatial spread of direct photoinhibition induced by GtACR1 was smaller than that produced by other photoinhibition methods.
claims.source: We tested the spatial spread of direct photoinhibition induced by GtACR1. In three different cortical regions, GtACR1-mediated photoinhibition also produced broad photoinhibition (Figure 6A), but the spatial spread was smaller than that produced by other photoinhibition methods (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing spatial spread of GtACR1-mediated photoinhibition (Figure 6A-B) with other methods (Figure 5J).

claims.claim: At 90% spike rate reduction near the laser center, the half-max radius of photoinhibition was 0.8 mm for GtACR1, compared to >1 mm for other methods.
claims.source: For example, at 90% spike rate reduction near the laser center, the half-max radius of photoinhibition was 0.8 mm, compared to >1 mm for other methods (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing photoinhibition strength versus spatial spread for GtACR1 compared to other methods (Figure 6B).

claims.claim: Local infection with Cre-dependent, ChR2-expressing virus in PV-IRES-Cre mice produced the smallest lateral spread in photoinhibition (radius, approximately 0.5 mm).
claims.source: To limit activation of interneurons we injected small volumes of Cre-dependent ChR2 virus in PV-IRES-Cre mice (Cardin et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2012; Lien and Scanziani, 2013; Pafundo et al., 2016). The virus injection localized the expression of ChR2 (diameter of expression, 500 µm, Figure 7A). Silicon probe recordings (Figure 7B) confirmed that photostimulation excited FS neurons only at the infection site (Figure 7C). In the surrounding regions, FS neuron spike rates were even slightly suppressed (e.g. Figure 7C, at 400 µm away). Photoinhibition of pyramidal neurons extended additional several hundred micrometers, with neurons suppressed even 800 µm away from the photostimulus center. At 90% spike rate reduction at the infection site, the half-max radius of photoinhibition was approximately 0.5 mm (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing spatial profile of photoinhibition with virus injection (Figure 7A-D).

claims.claim: Limiting the spatial extend of interneuron excitation reduced photoinhibition spread.
claims.source: Thus, limiting the spatial extend of interneuron excitation reduced photoinhibition spread.
claims.evidence: Inference based on comparison of photoinhibition spread with virus injection (Figure 7D) versus transgenic expression (Figure 5J).

claims.claim: Optogenetic inactivation methods have a fundamental resolution on the order of 1 mm.
claims.source: Overall these results suggest that optgogenetic inactivation methods have a fundamental resolution on the order of 1 mm (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: Inference based on summary of spatial spread measurements across all methods (Figure 8).

claims.claim: In regions surrounding the photostimulation site, a concurrent decrease in activity was observed in both FS neurons and pyramidal neurons, even with ChR-assisted photoinhibition.
claims.source: Consistent with this interpretation, in regions surrounding the photostimulation site, a concurrent decrease in activity was observed in both FS neurons and pyramidal neurons, even with ChR-assisted photoinhibition (Figure 9, arrows).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate versus lateral distance for both FS and pyramidal neurons (Figure 9).

claims.claim: Activity decreased in proportion in FS and pyramidal neurons relative to their baseline activity.
claims.source: Activity decreased in proportion in FS and pyramidal neurons relative to their baseline activity.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing parallel decreases in relative spike rate for FS and pyramidal neurons in the surround (Figure 9).

claims.claim: Inhibition-stabilized networks exhibit paradoxical effects where selective excitation of interneurons paradoxically decreases interneuron activity together with excitatory neurons.
claims.source: These inhibition-stabilized networks (ISN) exhibit paradoxical effects. Selective excitation of interneurons paradoxically decreases interneuron activity together with excitatory neurons (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2016; Pehlevan and Sompolinsky, 2014; Rubin et al., 2015; Sadeh et al., 2017; Tsodyks et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical studies of inhibition-stabilized networks.

claims.claim: Because of recurrent excitatory connectivity in cortical circuits, the effects on excitatory neuron spike rates are amplified, which causes a large reduction in excitation of inhibitory interneurons.
claims.source: Because of recurrent excitatory connectivity in cortical circuits, the effects on excitatory neuron spike rates are amplified, which causes a large reduction in excitation of inhibitory interneurons.
claims.evidence: Inference based on known properties of inhibition-stabilized networks and recurrent connectivity.

claims.claim: In mice expressing ReaChR in PV neurons, using orange light to illuminate a large part of the cortex, pyramidal neurons monotonically decreased their activity as a function of light intensity.
claims.source: In mice expressing ReaChR in PV neurons, we used orange light to illuminate a large part of the cortex (2 mm beam diameter at 4σ at the surface of the brain) to drive excitation in nearly all PV neurons across cortical layers (Figure 10A). Pyramidal neurons monotonically decreased their activity as a function of light intensity (Figure 10B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate as a function of light intensity for pyramidal neurons (Figure 10B).

claims.claim: FS neurons also decreased their activity, roughly in proportion despite being excited by ReaChR.
claims.source: Interestingly, FS neurons also decreased their activity, roughly in proportion despite being excited by ReaChR.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate as a function of light intensity for FS neurons (Figure 10B).

claims.claim: As a function of light intensity, activity in FS neurons continued to decrease until most of the pyramidal neuron activity was silenced (at 0.4 mW/mm2).
claims.source: As a function of light intensity, activity in FS neurons continued to decrease until most of the pyramidal neuron activity was silenced (Figure 10B, at 0.4 mW/mm2).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate as a function of light intensity (Figure 10B).

claims.claim: At higher light intensities the FS neuron activity increased, likely driven by an increased photocurrent and transition to a regime with little coupling due to lack of excitatory activity.
claims.source: At higher light intensities the FS neuron activity increased. This increase was likely driven by an increased photocurrent. In addition, the network also transitioned to a regime with little coupling due to lack of excitatory activity.
claims.evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing FS neuron activity increase at high light intensities (Figure 10B) and understanding of network dynamics.

claims.claim: The data are consistent with the paradoxical effect predicted by cortical circuit models stabilized by inhibition.
claims.source: These data are consistent with the paradoxical effect predicted by cortical circuit models stabilized by inhibition (Tsodyks et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: Inference based on comparison of experimental data (Figure 10) with predictions from cited theoretical models.

claims.claim: For ChR-assisted photoinhibition, the kinetics of ChR determined the dynamics of the interneurons.
claims.source: For ChR-assisted photoinhibition, the kinetics of ChR determined the dynamics of the interneurons (Figure 11A).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing different temporal dynamics for ChR2 versus ReaChR in FS neurons (Figure 11A).

claims.claim: In mice expressing ChR2 (VGAT-ChR2-EYFP), FS neuron activity was time-locked to the photostimulus.
claims.source: For example, in mice expressing ChR2 (VGAT-ChR2-EYFP), FS neuron activity was time-locked to the photostimulus.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing PSTH of FS neurons in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice (Figure 11A).

claims.claim: In mice expressing ReaChR (PV-IRES-Cre x ReaChR), which has slower off kinetics compared to ChR2, FS neuron activity was not time-locked to the photostimulus and was strongly attenuated over prolonged photostimulation.
claims.source: In mice expressing ReaChR (PV-IRES-Cre x ReaChR), which has slower off kinetics compared to ChR2 (Lin et al., 2012), FS neuron activity was not time-locked to the photostimulus and was strongly attenuated over prolonged photostimulation.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing PSTH of FS neurons in PV-IRES-Cre x ReaChR mice (Figure 11A) and citation to Lin et al., 2012 regarding ReaChR kinetics.

claims.claim: Despite the different interneuron dynamics, the photoinhibition of pyramidal neurons was similar.
claims.source: Despite the different interneuron dynamics, the photoinhibition of pyramidal neurons was similarly (Figure 11A).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing similar PSTH of pyramidal neurons for ChR2 and ReaChR (Figure 11A).

claims.claim: Prolonged photostimulation (>20 ms) triggered spikes in a subset of FS interneurons, which in turn reduced activity in other FS neurons and pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: These data suggest that prolonged photostimulation (>20 ms) triggered spikes in a subset of FS interneurons, which in turn reduced activity in other FS neurons and pyramidal neurons.
claims.evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing spike rate changes in FS neurons at different epochs (Figure 11B).

claims.claim: For ChR-assisted photoinhibition, the photoinhibition lagged FS neuron excitation by 3 ms.
claims.source: For ChR-assisted photoinhibition, the photoinhibition lagged FS neuron excitation by 3 ms (Materials and methods; at >1.5 mW, FS excitation onset, 1.1 ± 0.2 ms).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of PSTH data showing timing of FS excitation and pyramidal neuron inhibition.

claims.claim: Photoinhibition was detectable 4.0 ± 1.7 ms after photostimulation onset and reached a maximum at 18.4 ± 1.6 ms ('photoinhibition onset').
claims.source: Photoinhibition was detectable 4.0 ± 1.7 ms after photostimulation onset (mean ± s.e.m., based on t-test of spike counts against baseline) and reached a maximum at 18.4 ± 1.6 ms ('photoinhibition onset', Figure 11C).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of PSTH data (Figure 11C).

claims.claim: ChR2-assisted photoinhibition has a slightly faster onset (14.6 ms) than ReachR-assisted photoinhibition (18.8 ms).
claims.source: ChR2-assisted photoinhibition has a slightly faster onset (14.6 ms) than ReachR-assisted photoinhibition (18.8 ms; p<0.001, bootstrap, one-tailed test, Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of photoinhibition onset times (Figure 11C).

claims.claim: Direct hyperpolarization of pyramidal neurons using Arch produced even more rapid photoinhibition onset (5 ms).
claims.source: Direct hyperpolarization of pyramidal neurons using Arch produced even more rapid photoinhibition onset (5 ms, Figure 11C).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of photoinhibition onset times for Arch (Figure 11C).

claims.claim: Photoinhibition onset was progressively delayed at increasing distance from the laser center.
claims.source: Photoinhibition onset was progressively delayed at increasing distance from the laser center (Figure 11D–E).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing PSTH at different distances from photostimulus center (Figure 11E).

claims.claim: Photoinhibition at 2 mm away lagged the photoinhibition at the laser center by 10 ms.
claims.source: Photoinhibition at 2 mm away lagged the photoinhibition at the laser center by 10 ms (Figure 11E).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing photoinhibition onset latencies at different distances (Figure 11E).

claims.claim: This suggests a gradual spread of photoinhibition, consistent with the interpretation that coupling between cortical neurons mediated the photoinhibition spatial spread.
claims.source: This suggests a gradual spread of photoinhibition, consistent with the interpretation that coupling between cortical neurons mediated the photoinhibition spatial spread.
claims.evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing progressive delay in photoinhibition onset with distance (Figure 11E).

claims.claim: Removal of photoinhibition elevated spike rate above baseline ('rebound activity'), which decayed to baseline over hundreds of milliseconds.
claims.source: The temporal profile of photoinhibition offset was limited by rebound activity. Removal of photoinhibition elevated spike rate above baseline ('rebound activity'), which decayed to baseline over hundreds of milliseconds (Figure 12A).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing PSTH after photostimulation offset (Figure 12A).

claims.claim: Rebound activity depended on both photostimulus duration and intensity.
claims.source: Rebound activity depended on both photostimulus duration and intensity (Figure 12B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing spike rates before, during, and after photostimulation for different durations and powers (Figure 12B).

claims.claim: For short photostimulation durations, rebound activity was moderate regardless of photostimulus intensity (at 500 ms duration, rebound activity was 10% of baseline for 1.5–7 mW).
claims.source: For short photostimulation durations, rebound activity was moderate regardless of photostimulus intensity (Figure 12C, e.g. at 500 ms duration, rebound activity was 10% of baseline for 1.5–7 mW).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing rebound activity as a function of laser power and photostimulation duration (Figure 12C).

claims.claim: For long photostimulation durations, rebound activity was substantial even at low laser power (following a 4 s duration, rebound spike rate was >30% of baseline spike rate even at 1.5 mW).
claims.source: For long photostimulation durations, rebound activity was substantial even at low laser power (Figure 12C, e.g. following a 4 s duration, rebound spike rate was >30% of baseline spike rate even at 1.5 mW).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing rebound activity as a function of laser power and photostimulation duration (Figure 12C).

claims.claim: At moderate photostimulation duration (1 s), all photoinhibition methods produced some rebound activity regardless of photoinhibition strength.
claims.source: At moderate photostimulation duration (1 s), all photoinhibition methods produced some rebound activity regardless of photoinhibition strength (Figure 12D, Pearson's correlation, r = −0.2, p=0.29).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing rebound activity as a function of photoinhibition strength across different methods (Figure 12D).

claims.claim: The rebound activity could be caused by recovery from synaptic depression in silenced excitatory neurons, synaptic depression in activated FS neurons, or perturbed intracellular ion concentrations accumulated over prolonged duration of photostimulation.
claims.source: The rebound activity could be caused by recovery from synaptic depression in silenced excitatory neurons, synaptic depression in activated FS neurons, or perturbed intracellular ion concentrations accumulated over prolonged duration of photostimulation (Mahn et al., 2016; Wiegert et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms supported by citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: Photoinhibition onset was rapid (10 ms), but the offset was limited by rebound activity.
claims.source: In summary, photoinhibition onset was rapid (10 ms), but the offset was limited by rebound activity.
claims.evidence: Summary inference based on experimental data showing photoinhibition onset (Figure 11C) and rebound activity (Figure 12).

claims.claim: Attenuating the photostimulus gradually (100 ms) or reducing the photostimulus durations can both reduce rebound activity.
claims.source: Attenuating the photostimulus gradually (100 ms) or reducing the photostimulus durations can both reduce rebound activity (Figure 12).
claims.evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing relationship between photostimulus parameters and rebound activity (Figure 12).

claims.claim: The spatial resolution of optogenetic silencing is approximately one millimeter, with silencing spreading further than the photostimulation light.
claims.source: We found that the spatial resolution of optogenetic silencing is approximately one millimeter, with silencing spreading further than the photostimulation light.
claims.evidence: Summary inference based on experimental data showing spatial spread of photoinhibition across multiple methods (Figures 5-8).

claims.claim: The length scale of photoinhibition is caused by strong coupling within cortical circuits: loss of activity in a focal region withdraws input to other layers and surrounding regions, resulting in loss of activity in both excitatory and inhibitory populations in the surround.
claims.source: The length scale of photoinhibition is caused by strong coupling within cortical circuits: loss of activity in a focal region withdraws input to other layers and surrounding regions, resulting in loss of activity in both excitatory and inhibitory populations in the surround, as predicted by network models (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2016; Rubin et al., 2015; Sadeh et al., 2017; Tsodyks et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing concurrent decrease in FS and pyramidal neurons in surround (Figure 9) and citations to theoretical models.

claims.claim: At moderate laser powers (1.5 mW) photoinhibition in ChR2-EYFP mice was limited to cortex, with no obvious silencing in subcortical regions immediately below cortex.
claims.source: Consistent with this intensity distribution, at moderate laser powers (1.5 mW) photoinhibition in ChR2-EYFP mice was limited to cortex, with no obvious silencing in subcortical regions immediately below cortex (Guo et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: Inference based on light intensity distribution (Figure 3) and citation to previous study.

claims.claim: Higher light intensities in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice can cause photoinhibition in the hippocampus and striatum beneath cortical photostimulation sites.
claims.source: However, higher light intensities in these mice can cause photoinhibition in the hippocampus and striatum beneath cortical photostimulation sites (Babl et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Babl et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Silencing mediated by red light is more likely to cause wide-spread direct optogenetic effects compared to blue light, since red light penetrates deeper into the tissue.
claims.source: Silencing mediated by red light is more likely to cause wide-spread direct optogenetic effects compared to blue light, since red light penetrates deeper into the tissue (Lin et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Inference based on light penetration data (Figure 3) and citation to Lin et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Local expression of ChR limited the excitation of FS interneurons to a small region (~200 um in radius).
claims.source: Local expression of ChR limited the excitation of FS interneurons to a small region (~200 um in radius, Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing FS neuron excitation profile with virus injection (Figure 7C).

claims.claim: In regions surrounding the viral injection site, photostimulation caused a decrease in activity of both FS neurons and pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: For example, in regions surrounding the viral injection site, photostimulation caused a decrease in activity of both FS neurons and pyramidal neurons.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing FS neuron spike rates were slightly suppressed at 400 µm away from injection site (Figure 7C).

claims.claim: Similar withdrawal of input could potentially explain the uniform photoinhibition across layers.

results.result: ChR-assisted photoinhibition is more effective than direct photoinhibition using light-gated ion pumps (Arch and Jaws), achieving >80% spike rate reduction at lower laser powers (0.5-1.5 mW vs ~10-fold higher power).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9, and C10 collectively demonstrate that ChR-assisted photoinhibition requires significantly lower laser powers than Arch and Jaws to achieve similar levels of neuronal silencing. The experimental data from silicon probe recordings across multiple transgenic mouse lines (Figure 1E) provide strong quantitative evidence for this comparison.

results.result: GtACR1 produces the most potent photoinhibition among tested methods, achieving >80% spike silencing at 0.1 mW with minimal excitation below 0.2 mW, though transient axonal excitation occurs at higher powers.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C12, C13, and C14 are well-supported by experimental data showing GtACR1's superior sensitivity (Figure 2C-D). The characterization of power-dependent effects, including the identification of an optimal power range (0.05-0.3 mW) that avoids axonal excitation, provides comprehensive evidence for GtACR1's effectiveness and limitations.

results.result: Blue light (473 nm) is highly confined in cortical tissue with intensity dropping to <20% at 500 µm depth and 50% at 135 µm laterally, while orange light (594 nm) penetrates much further (depth at half max 846 µm), illuminating 28 times larger volume.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, and C8 are supported by direct photobleaching measurements in transgenic mice expressing fluorescent proteins in neuronal nuclei (Figure 3). The quantitative characterization of wavelength-dependent light propagation provides essential baseline data for interpreting optogenetic effects, though the authors acknowledge the measurements have limited dynamic range and may miss long tails in light intensity.

results.result: Photoinhibition spreads substantially beyond the photostimulation light (approximately 1 mm spatial resolution), extending beyond typical dendritic and axonal arbor sizes, with the fractional spike rate reduction near the laser center predicting lateral spread across methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C26, C27, C33, C38, and C68 are well-supported by extensive experimental data showing photoinhibition extending 1 mm beyond FS neuron activation profiles (Figures 5-8). The consistency of this finding across multiple optogenetic methods, brain regions, and wavelengths provides strong evidence for a fundamental spatial resolution limit of approximately 1 mm in cortical optogenetic inactivation.

results.result: GtACR1-mediated photoinhibition produces smaller spatial spread than other methods, with half-max radius of 0.8 mm at 90% spike rate reduction compared to >1 mm for other methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C34 and C35 are supported by experimental data comparing GtACR1 spatial spread across three cortical regions with other photoinhibition methods (Figure 6). The quantitative comparison demonstrates GtACR1's superior spatial resolution, though the spread still extends substantially beyond the light profile, indicating circuit-mediated effects remain important.

results.result: Local viral expression of ChR2 in PV neurons produces the smallest lateral spread of photoinhibition (radius approximately 0.5 mm at 90% reduction), limiting FS neuron excitation to ~200 µm radius while photoinhibition extends to 800 µm.
results.evaluation: Claims C36, C37, C73, and C74 are supported by experimental data from virus injection experiments (Figure 7). The demonstration that limiting the spatial extent of interneuron expression reduces but does not eliminate photoinhibition spread provides important evidence for circuit-mediated effects and offers a practical approach to improve spatial resolution.

results.result: In regions surrounding photostimulation, both FS and pyramidal neurons show concurrent proportional decreases in activity, indicating strong coupling within cortical circuits where loss of activity in a focal region withdraws input to surrounding regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C40, and C69 are supported by experimental data showing parallel decreases in FS and pyramidal neuron activity in the surround (Figure 9) and are consistent with predictions from inhibition-stabilized network models. The proportional decrease in both cell types provides strong evidence for circuit-mediated spread of inactivation rather than direct optical effects alone.

results.result: Over a range of light intensities, optogenetic excitation of PV neurons produces a 'paradoxical effect' where FS neurons decrease activity despite being excited, together with pyramidal neurons, consistent with inhibition-stabilized network predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C41-C47, and C81-C83 are well-supported by experimental data showing concurrent decreases in FS and pyramidal neuron activity during weak PV neuron photostimulation (Figure 10). The dose-dependent relationship and transition out of the paradoxical regime at high light intensities are consistent with theoretical predictions, though the detailed quantitative relationship remains to be fully explained.

results.result: ChR-assisted photoinhibition produces nearly uniform inhibition of pyramidal neurons across cortical layers (>80% spike reduction at 1.5-14 mW), with remarkably similar profiles for blue and orange light despite different light propagation.
results.evaluation: Claims C15, C16, C19, and C22 are supported by silicon probe recordings showing uniform photoinhibition across cortical depth (Figure 4). The similarity of inhibition profiles despite wavelength-dependent differences in light penetration provides strong evidence for circuit-mediated effects, though the mechanisms underlying uniform inhibition across layers require further investigation.

results.result: Photoinhibition offset is followed by rebound excitation that depends on both photostimulus duration and intensity, limiting temporal resolution, though rebound can be reduced by gradually attenuating the photostimulus or reducing duration.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C60-C64, C66, C67, and C104 are well-supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent rebound activity (Figure 12). The characterization of rebound activity across different photostimulation parameters and methods provides important practical guidance, though the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood.

results.result: The kinetics of channelrhodopsin variants determine interneuron dynamics (ChR2 produces time-locked activity, ReaChR shows attenuation), but pyramidal neuron photoinhibition is similar despite different interneuron dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 are supported by experimental data comparing temporal dynamics of ChR2 and ReaChR in FS neurons and resulting pyramidal neuron inhibition (Figure 11A). The finding that different interneuron dynamics produce similar pyramidal neuron inhibition suggests network-level compensation, though the mechanisms require further investigation.

results.result: ChR-assisted photoinhibition onset is rapid (photoinhibition detectable at 4.0±1.7 ms, maximum at 18.4±1.6 ms), with ChR2 slightly faster than ReaChR (14.6 vs 18.8 ms), while direct Arch-mediated photoinhibition is fastest (5 ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are supported by quantitative analysis of PSTH data (Figure 11C). The characterization of onset kinetics across different methods provides important practical information for experimental design, with appropriate statistical analysis supporting the comparison between ChR2 and ReaChR.

results.result: Photoinhibition onset is progressively delayed with increasing distance from the laser center (10 ms lag at 2 mm), suggesting gradual spread consistent with coupling between cortical neurons mediating spatial spread.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 are supported by experimental data showing distance-dependent delays in photoinhibition onset (Figure 11E). The progressive delay provides additional evidence for circuit-mediated spread of inactivation, though alternative explanations related to light propagation dynamics are not fully excluded.

results.result: At low laser powers (0.5 mW) in Sst-IRES-Cre x Ai32 mice, selective excitation of Sst neurons produces disinhibition of excitatory neurons around layer 4, likely mediated by Sst neurons inhibiting PV neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C17 and C18 are supported by experimental data showing increased relative spike rate in layer 4 at low power (Figure 4A) and inference based on known circuit connectivity. This finding highlights the complexity of optogenetic manipulations in actual neural networks, though the proposed mechanism requires direct validation.

results.result: At moderate laser power (1.5 mW), blue light excites FS neurons mainly in superficial layers, yet loss of activity is present in both superficial and deep layers, suggesting circuit-mediated effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C21, and C76 are supported by comparison of FS neuron excitation profiles (Figure 4C) with pyramidal neuron inhibition across layers (Figure 4A) and light penetration data (Figure 3). The mismatch between direct optical effects and functional inhibition provides evidence for circuit-mediated spread, though the specific mechanisms require further investigation.

results.result: For Arch-mediated photoinhibition, temporally-modulated photostimuli (40 Hz sinusoid) are more effective in silencing activity than constant photostimuli at the same average power.
results.evaluation: Claim C11 is supported by experimental data comparing different photostimulus profiles (Figure 1F). This finding provides practical guidance for optimizing Arch-mediated photoinhibition, though the underlying mechanisms are not explored.

results.result: FS neuron activation in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice is dose-dependent with lateral spread dependent on laser power (half-max width 0.15 mm at 0.5 mW, 1.5 mm at 14 mW), indicating long tails in light intensity can activate channels >1 mm from laser center.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are supported by experimental data showing power-dependent FS neuron excitation profiles (Figure 5B). The finding that FS neurons can be activated at distances exceeding predictions from photobleaching measurements highlights limitations of the photobleaching assay and importance of direct functional measurements.

results.result: Photoinhibition profiles are similarly broad across different methods (selective PV or Sst neuron excitation, direct photoinhibition with Arch/Jaws, different brain regions) regardless of the specific approach used.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 are supported by experimental data comparing photoinhibition profiles across multiple methods and brain regions (Figure 5C-I). The consistency of broad spatial spread across diverse approaches provides strong evidence for circuit-mediated effects as a fundamental property of cortical photoinhibition.

results.result: Prolonged photostimulation (>20 ms) triggers spikes in a subset of FS interneurons, which in turn reduces activity in other FS neurons and pyramidal neurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C52 is an inference based on experimental data showing different FS neuron responses at different epochs (Figure 11B). While the data show heterogeneous FS neuron responses, the proposed mechanism of subset-mediated inhibition is speculative and requires direct validation through simultaneous recordings or other approaches.

results.result: Rebound activity could be caused by recovery from synaptic depression in silenced excitatory neurons, synaptic depression in activated FS neurons, or perturbed intracellular ion concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 is speculation about possible mechanisms supported by citations to relevant literature. While the proposed mechanisms are plausible, no direct experimental evidence is provided to distinguish between these alternatives or confirm any specific mechanism.

results.result: Withdrawal of input could potentially explain uniform photoinhibition across layers, particularly for blue light mediated ChR-assisted photoinhibition.
results.evaluation: Claim C75 is speculation about mechanism supported by citations and reference to experimental data (Figure 4A). While the proposed mechanism is consistent with the data, it remains speculative without direct experimental validation of input withdrawal and its layer-specific effects.

results.result: Cortical neurons require thalamic drive to maintain activity, and silencing cortex reduces thalamic activity, suggesting intracortical connections might also be required to maintain cortical activity in addition to thalamocortical input.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 combine cited prior work with inferences about the current data. While the citations support the importance of thalamocortical interactions, the inference about intracortical connections' role is speculative and requires direct experimental validation through simultaneous cortical and thalamic recordings during photoinhibition.

results.result: Previous studies did not find the paradoxical effect, possibly because they manipulated only subsets of PV neurons using viral expression, whereas this study weakly photostimulated nearly all PV neurons in superficial layers, and the effect requires exciting a large proportion of interneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 compare current results with previous studies and propose explanations for discrepancies. While the comparison is informative and the proposed explanations are plausible based on theoretical predictions, direct experimental validation comparing subset vs. population-wide manipulation in the same preparation would be needed to definitively establish this explanation.

results.result: At moderate laser powers (1.5 mW), photoinhibition in ChR2-EYFP mice is limited to cortex with no obvious subcortical silencing, but higher powers can cause photoinhibition in hippocampus and striatum; red light is more likely to cause widespread direct effects due to deeper penetration.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 combine inference from light intensity distribution with citations to prior studies. The inference about moderate power effects is supported by light penetration data (Figure 3) and citation to Guo et al., 2014b, while the statement about higher powers is supported by citation to Babl et al., 2019. The inference about red light is logical given the penetration data.

results.result: Data were collected under awake non-behaving conditions, but previous studies found little difference in photoinhibition strength across behavioral conditions.
results.evaluation: Claim C90 describes experimental conditions and cites previous studies showing consistency across behavioral states. This provides important context for interpreting the results and their generalizability, supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: ChR-assisted and GtACR1-mediated photoinhibition produce complete silencing near the laser center across a large power range (1.5-10 mW), but spatial spread differs substantially with power, producing graded loss-of-function manipulations that correlate with behavioral effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C95 are supported by experimental data showing power-dependent spatial spread (Figures 5-6) and citation to behavioral study (Guo et al., 2014b). The characterization of power-dependent effects provides important practical guidance for experimental design, linking spatial spread to functional consequences.

results.result: The 1 mm spatial resolution of photoinhibition poses a limit on loss-of-function manipulations in neocortex, requiring interpretation that accounts for spatial spread; systematic mapping and deconvolution could help recover the underlying region involved in behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 draw practical implications from the spatial spread findings and propose experimental approaches. The inferences about limitations and false-positives are logical consequences of the data, and the proposed deconvolution approach is supported by citation to Li et al., 2016.

results.result: Sub-millimeter resolution might be achievable with more sensitive effectors and patterned illumination; spatial resolution could differ across brain regions due to differences in GABAergic projections and recurrent excitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 are speculation about future possibilities and regional differences. While the speculations are reasonable based on known circuit differences, they lack direct experimental support and represent hypotheses for future testing rather than established findings.

results.result: Rebound activity can be partially alleviated by changes in photostimulus parameters; cell-type-specific manipulations produce multi-phasic network responses over hundreds of milliseconds, highlighting the need to measure effects on both local and downstream circuits in behaving animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 combine experimental findings with citations to previous studies and draw practical implications. The statement about parameter optimization is supported by experimental data (Figure 12C) and citation, while the broader implications are supported by citations to studies examining downstream effects.
